title: Strings
bridge: A C string is an array of `char` ending with a hidden `'\0'` (zero) that marks the end. `strlen(s)` counts up to it; `strcpy`, `strcat`, `strcmp` come from `<string.h>`. You can't use `==` to compare strings (that compares addresses): use `strcmp(a, b) == 0`.
lesson:
```
char crop[10] = "maize";   /* m a i z e \0, with room to spare */
strlen(crop);              /* 5: counts up to the \0 */
crop[0] = 'M';             /* "Maize" */
```

The `'\0'` at the end is how every string function knows where to stop. If it's missing, they keep reading into random memory.

From `<string.h>`:

```
strcmp(a, b) == 0      /* same text? (NOT a == b) */
strcpy(dest, src);     /* copy: dest must be big enough! */
strcat(dest, src);     /* add on the end: same warning */
```

From `<ctype.h>`: `toupper(c)`, `tolower(c)`, `isdigit(c)`, `isalpha(c)`, `isspace(c)`.

Walking a string is a loop until the `\0`:

```
for (int i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++) {
    s[i] = toupper(s[i]);
}
```

`const char *s` means "a string I'll only read". A string literal like `"maize"` must not be changed, so functions that change text need a real array (`char s[] = "maize";`).

exercises.title: Count vowels
exercises.prompt: Write int count_vowels(const char *s): how many a, e, i, o, u (either case).

exercises.title: Shout in place
exercises.prompt: Write char *shout(char *s) that changes s to capitals in place and returns s.
hints: Loop to the '\0', changing each char.

quiz.q: How does C know where a string ends?
choices: A '\0' character after the last letter
